claim: Mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake is mediated by an inner mitochondrial membrane protein called the mitochondrial calcium uniporter.
source: Mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake is mediated by an inner mitochondrial membrane protein called the mitochondrial calcium uniporter.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: In humans, the uniporter functions as a holocomplex consisting of MCU, EMRE, MICU1 and MICU2.
source: In humans, the uniporter functions as a holocomplex consisting of MCU, EMRE, MICU1 and MICU2, among which MCU and EMRE form a subcomplex and function as the conductive channel while MICU1 and MICU2 are EF-hand proteins that regulate the channel activity in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MCU and EMRE form a subcomplex and function as the conductive channel.
source: In humans, the uniporter functions as a holocomplex consisting of MCU, EMRE, MICU1 and MICU2, among which MCU and EMRE form a subcomplex and function as the conductive channel while MICU1 and MICU2 are EF-hand proteins that regulate the channel activity in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by previous structural studies cited in the manuscript and the current structural data.

claim: MICU1 and MICU2 are EF-hand proteins that regulate the channel activity in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: In humans, the uniporter functions as a holocomplex consisting of MCU, EMRE, MICU1 and MICU2, among which MCU and EMRE form a subcomplex and function as the conductive channel while MICU1 and MICU2 are EF-hand proteins that regulate the channel activity in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by the structural observations and functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Ca2+ changes the dimerization interaction between MICU1 and MICU2.
source: Our structural observations suggest that Ca2+ changes the dimerization interaction between MICU1 and MICU2, which in turn determines how the MICU1-MICU2 subcomplex interacts with the MCU-EMRE channel and, consequently, changes the distribution of the uniplex assemblies between the blocked and unblocked states.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structural data comparing Ca2+-bound and Ca2+-free states.

claim: The change in MICU1-MICU2 dimerization determines how the MICU1-MICU2 subcomplex interacts with the MCU-EMRE channel.
source: Our structural observations suggest that Ca2+ changes the dimerization interaction between MICU1 and MICU2, which in turn determines how the MICU1-MICU2 subcomplex interacts with the MCU-EMRE channel and, consequently, changes the distribution of the uniplex assemblies between the blocked and unblocked states.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison of different uniplex assemblies.

claim: Ca2+-dependent changes in MICU1-MICU2 interaction change the distribution of the uniplex assemblies between the blocked and unblocked states.
source: Our structural observations suggest that Ca2+ changes the dimerization interaction between MICU1 and MICU2, which in turn determines how the MICU1-MICU2 subcomplex interacts with the MCU-EMRE channel and, consequently, changes the distribution of the uniplex assemblies between the blocked and unblocked states.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of different structural states in the presence and absence of Ca2+.

claim: The mitochondrial network takes up large amounts of Ca2+ from its environment and buffers cytosolic Ca2+ elevations.
source: It has long been observed that the vast mitochondrial network takes up large amounts of Ca2+ from its environment and buffers cytosolic Ca2+ elevations, thus regulating the spatial and temporal dynamics of intracellular Ca2+ signaling (Clapham, 2007; Kamer and Mootha, 2015; Rizzuto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a well-established observation in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mitochondrial calcium uptake is mediated by the mitochondrial calcium uniporter, a Ca2+-selective channel localized to the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: Mitochondrial calcium uptake is mediated by the mitochondrial calcium uniporter, a Ca2+-selective channel that is localized to the inner mitochondrial membrane (Gunter and Pfeiffer, 1990; Kirichok et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: MCU is the pore-forming subunit of the uniporter.
source: In humans, the uniporter functions as a holocomplex (referred to as uniplex henceforth) and consists of the pore-forming subunit MCU (Baughman et al., 2011; De Stefani et al., 2011), an essential membrane-spanning subunit EMRE (Sancak et al., 2013), and the gate-keeping subunits MICU1 (Perocchi et al., 2010) and MICU2 (Plovanich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies that identified MCU as the pore-forming subunit.

claim: EMRE is an essential membrane-spanning subunit of the uniporter.
source: In humans, the uniporter functions as a holocomplex (referred to as uniplex henceforth) and consists of the pore-forming subunit MCU (Baughman et al., 2011; De Stefani et al., 2011), an essential membrane-spanning subunit EMRE (Sancak et al., 2013), and the gate-keeping subunits MICU1 (Perocchi et al., 2010) and MICU2 (Plovanich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies that identified EMRE as essential for uniporter function.

claim: MICU1 and MICU2 are gate-keeping subunits of the uniporter.
source: In humans, the uniporter functions as a holocomplex (referred to as uniplex henceforth) and consists of the pore-forming subunit MCU (Baughman et al., 2011; De Stefani et al., 2011), an essential membrane-spanning subunit EMRE (Sancak et al., 2013), and the gate-keeping subunits MICU1 (Perocchi et al., 2010) and MICU2 (Plovanich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: MCU forms a tetrameric channel pore.
source: The two-transmembrane (2-TM) MCU component forms a tetrameric channel pore and the single-TM EMRE becomes an integral part of the channel by forming a 1:1 stoichiometric subcomplex with MCU and renders the channel conductive (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited structural study and the current structural data.

claim: EMRE forms a 1:1 stoichiometric subcomplex with MCU and renders the channel conductive.
source: The two-transmembrane (2-TM) MCU component forms a tetrameric channel pore and the single-TM EMRE becomes an integral part of the channel by forming a 1:1 stoichiometric subcomplex with MCU and renders the channel conductive (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited structural study.

claim: An MCU-EMRE subcomplex constitutes the minimal component necessary and sufficient for mitochondrial calcium uptake.
source: Thus, an MCU-EMRE subcomplex constitutes the minimal component necessary and sufficient for mitochondrial calcium uptake (Kovács-Bogdán et al., 2014; Sancak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: MICU1 and MICU2 are localized to the mitochondrial intermembrane space.
source: MICU1 and MICU2 are two paralogous EF-hand containing proteins that are localized to the mitochondrial intermembrane space (IMS) and function as gate-keepers by sensing the cytosolic Ca2+ concentration and, thereby, regulate MCU-EMRE channel activity (Csordás et al., 2013; Kamer et al., 2017; Mallilankaraman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on MICU1 and MICU2 localization.

claim: MICU1 and MICU2 function as gate-keepers by sensing the cytosolic Ca2+ concentration.
source: MICU1 and MICU2 are two paralogous EF-hand containing proteins that are localized to the mitochondrial intermembrane space (IMS) and function as gate-keepers by sensing the cytosolic Ca2+ concentration and, thereby, regulate MCU-EMRE channel activity (Csordás et al., 2013; Kamer et al., 2017; Mallilankaraman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: Each MICU subunit contains four EF-hand motifs.
source: Each MICU subunit contains four EF-hand motifs among which only EF-1 and EF-4 are canonical and bind Ca2+, whereas EF-2 and EF-3 lack the essential residues for Ca2+ binding.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of MICU proteins.

claim: Only EF-1 and EF-4 of MICU subunits are canonical and bind Ca2+.
source: Each MICU subunit contains four EF-hand motifs among which only EF-1 and EF-4 are canonical and bind Ca2+, whereas EF-2 and EF-3 lack the essential residues for Ca2+ binding.
evidence: This is based on structural and biochemical analysis.

claim: EF-2 and EF-3 of MICU subunits lack the essential residues for Ca2+ binding.
source: Each MICU subunit contains four EF-hand motifs among which only EF-1 and EF-4 are canonical and bind Ca2+, whereas EF-2 and EF-3 lack the essential residues for Ca2+ binding.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: MICU1 and MICU2 form heterodimers with a disulfide bond between them.
source: Functional and biochemical analyses seem to converge on the following observations: MICU1 and MICU2 form heterodimers with a disulfide bond between them (Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Patron et al., 2014); MICU1 but not MICU2 interacts with the MCU pore (Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Plovanich et al., 2013), which is mediated by EMRE through electrostatic interactions between positively charged residues (KKKKR poly-basic region) at the N-terminus of MICU1 and the C-terminal poly-aspartate tail of EMRE (Tsai et al., 2016); recent studies also suggested that MICU1 makes direct interaction with the aspartate ring (D-ring) of MCU formed by the canonical DIME motif in the selectivity filter of an MCU channel tetramer (Paillard et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited biochemical studies.

claim: MICU1 but not MICU2 interacts with the MCU pore.
source: Functional and biochemical analyses seem to converge on the following observations: MICU1 and MICU2 form heterodimers with a disulfide bond between them (Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Patron et al., 2014); MICU1 but not MICU2 interacts with the MCU pore (Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Plovanich et al., 2013), which is mediated by EMRE through electrostatic interactions between positively charged residues (KKKKR poly-basic region) at the N-terminus of MICU1 and the C-terminal poly-aspartate tail of EMRE (Tsai et al., 2016); recent studies also suggested that MICU1 makes direct interaction with the aspartate ring (D-ring) of MCU formed by the canonical DIME motif in the selectivity filter of an MCU channel tetramer (Paillard et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional and biochemical studies.

claim: MICU1 interaction with MCU is mediated by EMRE through electrostatic interactions between the KKKKR poly-basic region at the N-terminus of MICU1 and the C-terminal poly-aspartate tail of EMRE.
source: Functional and biochemical analyses seem to converge on the following observations: MICU1 and MICU2 form heterodimers with a disulfide bond between them (Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Patron et al., 2014); MICU1 but not MICU2 interacts with the MCU pore (Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Plovanich et al., 2013), which is mediated by EMRE through electrostatic interactions between positively charged residues (KKKKR poly-basic region) at the N-terminus of MICU1 and the C-terminal poly-aspartate tail of EMRE (Tsai et al., 2016); recent studies also suggested that MICU1 makes direct interaction with the aspartate ring (D-ring) of MCU formed by the canonical DIME motif in the selectivity filter of an MCU channel tetramer (Paillard et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies and confirmed by the structural data in this manuscript.

claim: MICU1 makes direct interaction with the aspartate ring (D-ring) of MCU formed by the canonical DIME motif in the selectivity filter.
source: Functional and biochemical analyses seem to converge on the following observations: MICU1 and MICU2 form heterodimers with a disulfide bond between them (Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Patron et al., 2014); MICU1 but not MICU2 interacts with the MCU pore (Kamer and Mootha, 2014; Plovanich et al., 2013), which is mediated by EMRE through electrostatic interactions between positively charged residues (KKKKR poly-basic region) at the N-terminus of MICU1 and the C-terminal poly-aspartate tail of EMRE (Tsai et al., 2016); recent studies also suggested that MICU1 makes direct interaction with the aspartate ring (D-ring) of MCU formed by the canonical DIME motif in the selectivity filter of an MCU channel tetramer (Paillard et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by recent cited studies and confirmed by the structural data in this manuscript.

claim: At low cytosolic Ca2+ concentrations, MICU1 functions as a pore blocker and prevents Ca2+ uptake into the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Thus, the current model of MCU gating posits that at low cytosolic Ca2+ concentrations, MICU1 functions as a pore blocker and prevents Ca2+ uptake into the mitochondrial matrix and that MCU becomes disinhibited only when cytosolic Ca2+ approaches the micromolar range, resulting from cooperative Ca2+ binding to the EF-hands of MICU1 and MICU2 (Csordás et al., 2013; Kamer et al., 2017; Mallilankaraman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is the current model in the field, supported by cited functional studies and the structural data in this manuscript.

claim: MCU becomes disinhibited when cytosolic Ca2+ approaches the micromolar range.
source: Thus, the current model of MCU gating posits that at low cytosolic Ca2+ concentrations, MICU1 functions as a pore blocker and prevents Ca2+ uptake into the mitochondrial matrix and that MCU becomes disinhibited only when cytosolic Ca2+ approaches the micromolar range, resulting from cooperative Ca2+ binding to the EF-hands of MICU1 and MICU2 (Csordás et al., 2013; Kamer et al., 2017; Mallilankaraman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: MCU disinhibition results from cooperative Ca2+ binding to the EF-hands of MICU1 and MICU2.
source: Thus, the current model of MCU gating posits that at low cytosolic Ca2+ concentrations, MICU1 functions as a pore blocker and prevents Ca2+ uptake into the mitochondrial matrix and that MCU becomes disinhibited only when cytosolic Ca2+ approaches the micromolar range, resulting from cooperative Ca2+ binding to the EF-hands of MICU1 and MICU2 (Csordás et al., 2013; Kamer et al., 2017; Mallilankaraman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: Deleterious effects of aberrant mitochondrial calcium signaling are manifested in patients and animal models with defects in MICU1 rather than MCU.
source: Intriguingly, the deleterious effects of aberrant mitochondrial calcium signaling are manifested only in patients and animal models with defects in MICU1 rather than MCU (Bick et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2016; Logan et al., 2014; Musa et al., 2019), thus highlighting the impetus to pursue a better mechanistic understanding of the gating properties of the uniplex.
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical and animal studies.

claim: Multiple structures of individual components or subcomplexes of the uniporter have been determined.
source: Since the molecular identification of the uniplex composition, multiple structures of individual components or subcomplexes have been determined, including several fungal MCU orthologs (Baradaran et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2018), the human MCU-EMRE subcomplex (Wang et al., 2019) and the mammalian MICU1 and MICU2 proteins in the homo- and heterodimeric forms (Kamer et al., 2019; Park et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited structural studies.

claim: Several groups have recently reported structures of the MCU holocomplex in various states.
source: To this end, several groups have recently reported the structures of the MCU holocomplex in various states, including the structures of the human MCU holocomplex in low and high [Ca2+] (Fan et al., 2020), the structure of human MCU holocomplex in the absence of Ca2+ (Zhuo et al., 2020), and the structure of a holocomplex formed by the beetle MCU-EMRE and the human MICU1-MICU2 under resting [Ca2+] conditions (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited recent structural studies.

claim: The cryo-EM structures of the human MCU holocomplex reveal multiple, distinct uniplex assemblies.
source: Our structural study reveals multiple, distinct uniplex assemblies that likely represent the different functional states of the uniporter and provides structural insights into the Ca2+-dependent gate-keeping function of MICU1 and MICU2.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The distinct uniplex assemblies likely represent different functional states of the uniporter.
source: Our structural study reveals multiple, distinct uniplex assemblies that likely represent the different functional states of the uniporter and provides structural insights into the Ca2+-dependent gate-keeping function of MICU1 and MICU2.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and functional context.

claim: Four MCU subunits form the ion conduction pore, which is stabilized by four EMRE subunits that sit on the periphery.
source: Our previous structural study demonstrated that human MCU and EMRE together function as a conductive channel by assembling into a tightly packed subcomplex in which four MCU subunits form the ion conduction pore, which is stabilized by four EMRE subunits that sits on the periphery (Wang et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cited previous structural study and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two MCU-EMRE subcomplexes can dimerize through electrostatic interactions along an interface at the N-terminal domain of MCU.
source: Two MCU-EMRE subcomplexes can further dimerize through electrostatic interactions along an interface at the N-terminal domain of MCU.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: The SEC elution volume of the purified uniplex indicates a size much larger than the dimeric form of the MCU-EMRE subcomplex.
source: The SEC elution volume of the purified uniplex indicates a size much larger than the dimeric form of the MCU-EMRE subcomplex, suggesting that the uniplex also forms a dimer in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on the SEC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The uniplex forms a dimer in solution.
source: The SEC elution volume of the purified uniplex indicates a size much larger than the dimeric form of the MCU-EMRE subcomplex, suggesting that the uniplex also forms a dimer in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the SEC data.

claim: In the presence of Ca2+, the major class of uniplex particles shows a V-shaped dimer of MCU-EMRE subcomplexes with their tops bridged by a heterotetramer of MICU1 and MICU2.
source: 3D classification of the uniplex sample prepared in the presence of Ca2+ yielded one major class that shows clear density of a V-shaped dimer of the MCU-EMRE subcomplexes with their tops bridged by a heterotetramer of MICU1 and MICU2 (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The final EM map of the Ca2+-bound uniplex was refined to 4.2 Å.
source: To better resolve the MICU1 and MICU2 in the uniplex, we subsequently performed focused 3D classification by masking around the region of the MICU1-MICU2 heterotetramer, and the final EM map was refined to 4.2 Å (Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in the data processing workflow.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+, the uniplex particles are heterogeneous and can be classified into four classes with distinct conformations.
source: On the contrary, the particles of the uniplex sample prepared in the absence of Ca2+ were heterogeneous and could be classified into four classes with distinct conformations, indicating a diverse spectrum of uniplex assemblies (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The major class of apo uniplex particles represents a blocked uniplex in which a heterodimer of MICU1 and MICU2 blocks the central ion conduction pore of a monomeric MCU-EMRE subcomplex.
source: The major class of particles (class 1) represents a blocked uniplex in which a heterodimer of MICU1 and MICU2 blocks the central ion conduction pore of a monomeric MCU-EMRE subcomplex.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: In class 2 of apo uniplex, MICU1-MICU2 blocking is observed with the MCU-EMRE subcomplex retaining its dimeric form.
source: Similar MICU1-MICU2 blocking is also observed in the second class (class 2) with the exception being that MCU-EMRE subcomplex retains its dimeric form.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: The structure of the blocked uniplex was determined at 4.6 Å resolution.
source: By C2 symmetry expansion, particles of this class were combined with those of class one and yielded the structure of a blocked uniplex at 4.6 Å resolution (Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5, and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in the data processing workflow.

claim: In class 3 of apo uniplex, MICU1 and MICU2 form a heterotetramer and bridge the dimeric form of the MCU-EMRE subcomplex.
source: In the EM-map of class three that was determined at 4.7 Å, MICU1 and MICU2 form a heterotetramer and bridge the dimeric form of the MCU-EMRE subcomplex similar to that observed in the Ca2+-bound uniplex.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: Class 4 of apo uniplex represents a competing conformation in which both the MICU1-MICU2 heterotetramer as a bridge and the MICU1-MICU2 heterodimers as pore blockers are bound to the same MCU-EMRE subcomplex dimer.
source: Interestingly, the structure of class four represents a competing conformation in which both the MICU1-MICU2 heterotetramer – as a bridge – and the MICU1-MICU2 heterodimers – as pore blockers – are bound to the same MCU-EMRE subcomplex dimer.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: In class 4 of apo uniplex, the bridging MICU1-MICU2 tetramer is tilted to the side of the MCU-EMRE subcomplex due to competition.
source: Because of this competition, the bridging MICU1-MICU2 tetramer is tilted to the side of the MCU-EMRE subcomplex.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: The MCU-EMRE subcomplex is the most stable part of the uniplex.
source: In all these structures, the MCU-EMRE subcomplex appears to be the most stable part of the uniplex, as indicated by the well-defined density, whereas MICU1 and MICU2 are more dynamic and engage in the uniplex assembly with different configurations depending on the presence or absence of Ca2+.
evidence: This is inferred from the quality of the EM density in different regions of the structure.

claim: MICU1 and MICU2 are more dynamic and engage in the uniplex assembly with different configurations depending on the presence or absence of Ca2+.
source: In all these structures, the MCU-EMRE subcomplex appears to be the most stable part of the uniplex, as indicated by the well-defined density, whereas MICU1 and MICU2 are more dynamic and engage in the uniplex assembly with different configurations depending on the presence or absence of Ca2+.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of multiple conformations and variable density quality.

claim: In the presence of Ca2+, the uniplex adopts a two-fold symmetry.
source: In the presence of Ca2+, the uniplex adopts a two-fold symmetry and consists of a V-shaped dimer of MCU-EMRE subcomplexes and a MICU1-MICU2 heterotetramer that bridges the tops of the two subcomplexes (Figure 2a&b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 2a&b.

claim: The MICU1-MICU2 tetramer is formed by the dimerization of two MICU1-MICU2 heterodimers through a back-to-back packing between MICU2 subunits.
source: The MICU1-MICU2 tetramer is formed by the dimerization of two MICU1-MICU2 heterodimers through a back-to-back packing between MICU2 subunits (Xing et al., 2019), resulting in a linear arrangement of MICU1-MICU2-MICU2-MICU1.
evidence: This is observed in the structure and supported by a cited study.

claim: MICU1 and MICU2 dimerize through a face-to-face contact in which the EF-1 motif of one subunit interacts with the EF-3 of the other.
source: MICU1 and MICU2 dimerize through a face-to-face contact in which the EF-1 motif of one subunit interacts with the EF-3 of the other (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The face-to-face dimerization mode has been commonly observed in crystal structures of MICU1 and MICU2 homodimers as well as the MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer.
source: This face-to-face dimerization mode has been commonly observed in the crystal structures of MICU1 and MICU2 homodimers as well as the MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer (Park et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited crystal structures.

claim: Major Ca2+-induced conformational changes occur at the interface between MICU1 and MICU2.
source: Major Ca2+-induced conformational changes also occur at the interface between MICU1 and MICU2 as will be further discussed later.
evidence: This is observed in the structural comparison between apo and Ca2+-bound states.

claim: The assembly of the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer and MCU-EMRE subcomplexes in the presence of Ca2+ is mediated by interactions between MICU1 and EMRE.
source: The assembly of the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer and MCU-EMRE subcomplexes in the presence of Ca2+ is mediated by the interactions between MICU1 and EMRE.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: Each MICU1 subunit interacts with two EMRE subunits that are proximal to the central axis of the uniplex dimer by forming putative salt-bridge networks.
source: Each MICU1 subunit interacts with two EMRE subunits that are proximal to the central axis of the uniplex dimer by forming putative salt-bridge networks (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 2d–f.

claim: The α1 helix of MICU1 is oriented parallel to the membrane surface with its N-terminus pointing toward the C-terminal end of the transmembrane helix of EMRE.
source: Firstly, the α1 helix of MICU1 is oriented parallel to the membrane surface with its N-terminus pointing toward the C-terminal end of the transmembrane helix of EMRE (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The close proximity of the KKKKR poly-basic region of MICU1 and the C-terminal poly-aspartate tail of EMRE implies the formation of a network of salt bridges.
source: This configuration would lead to the convergence of the KKKKR poly-basic region that extends from the MICU1 α1 helix to the C-terminal poly-aspartate tail on EMRE. Although these two charged regions are not resolved in the structure, their close proximity would imply the formation of a network of salt bridges between them.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement and the known properties of these charged regions.

claim: Both the KKKKR poly-basic region of MICU1 and the C-terminal poly-aspartate tail of EMRE are highly conserved and important for uniplex assembly and Ca2+ uptake.
source: Both charged regions are highly conserved and have been shown to be important for uniplex assembly and Ca2+ uptake (Tsai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited functional study.

claim: The second point of contact between MICU1 and MCU-EMRE is mediated by the α11 helix of MICU1 and the poly-aspartate tail of another EMRE subunit.
source: The second point of contact is mediated by the α11 helix of MICU1 and the poly-aspartate tail of the other EMRE subunit.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: The poly-aspartate tail of EMRE forms an extended loop that runs parallel to and is positioned below the α11 helix of MICU1.
source: At this site, the poly-aspartate tail of EMRE forms an extended loop that runs parallel to and is positioned below the α11 helix of MICU1 (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The α11 helix of MICU1 contains multiple basic residues whose side chains point toward the EMRE loop and likely form salt bridges with the poly-aspartate tail of EMRE.
source: The MICU1 α11 helix contains multiple basic residues whose side chains point directly toward the EMRE loop and likely form the second network of salt bridges with the poly-aspartate tail of EMRE.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement.

claim: The binding of the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer does not block the channel pore of MCU.
source: The binding of the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer does not block the channel pore of MCU, nor does it introduce any visible conformational change to each MCU-EMRE subcomplex, whose structure is virtually identical to that determined previously without bound MICU1 and MICU2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures with and without MICU1-MICU2 binding.

claim: The binding of the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer does not introduce any visible conformational change to each MCU-EMRE subcomplex.
source: The binding of the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer does not block the channel pore of MCU, nor does it introduce any visible conformational change to each MCU-EMRE subcomplex, whose structure is virtually identical to that determined previously without bound MICU1 and MICU2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The uniplex structure obtained in the presence of Ca2+ represents the unblocked state in which the channel pore is poised for Ca2+ uptake.
source: Thus, the uniplex structure obtained in the presence of Ca2+ represents the unblocked state in which the channel pore is poised for Ca2+ uptake.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that the pore is not blocked.

claim: The tethering of two MCU-EMRE subcomplexes by the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer results in a slightly narrower V-shaped dimer compared to the subcomplex dimer without MICU1-MICU2.
source: However, the tethering of two MCU-EMRE subcomplexes by the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer appears to exert a pulling force on the MCU-EMRE subcomplexes, resulting in a slightly narrower V-shaped dimer as compared to the subcomplex dimer structure previously determined without MICU1-MICU2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The blocking of the central channel pore by a MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer is the dominant form of uniplex assembly in the absence of Ca2+.
source: Multiple uniplex assemblies were observed in the absence of Ca2+, among which the blocking of the central channel pore by a MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer is the dominant form.
evidence: This is observed in the particle distribution from cryo-EM data.

claim: MICU1-MICU2 blocking occurs on both the monomeric and dimeric forms of the MCU-EMRE subcomplex.
source: This MICU1-MICU2 blocking event occurs on both the monomeric and dimeric forms of the MCU-EMRE subcomplex.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: The particles of blocked monomeric subcomplex likely come from the dissociation of the subcomplex dimer during EM grid preparation.
source: As the MCU-EMRE subcomplex remained dimeric in the purified uniplex sample, we suspect that the particles of blocked monomeric subcomplex likely come from the dissociation of the subcomplex dimer during EM grid preparation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the purified sample is dimeric but monomers are observed on the grid.

claim: With four-fold symmetry at the channel pore of MCU-EMRE, the MICU1-MICU2 dimer can bind and block the channel in four possible orientations.
source: With four-fold symmetry at the channel pore of MCU-EMRE, the MICU1-MICU2 dimer can bind and block the channel in four possible orientations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the symmetry of the MCU pore and observed in the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the blocked uniplex structure, MICU1 engages with the MCU-EMRE subcomplex at three major points of contact using its N- and C-terminal helices.
source: In the blocked uniplex structure, MICU1 engages with the MCU-EMRE subcomplex at three major points of contact using its N- and C-terminal helices (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The α1 helix of MICU1 is oriented directly above the ion conduction pore with its N-terminus pointing toward the C-terminus of the EMRE helix in the blocked uniplex.
source: Firstly, the α1 helix of MICU1 is oriented directly above the ion conduction pore with its N-terminus pointing toward the C-terminus of the EMRE helix.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: In the blocked uniplex, the N-terminal poly-basic region of MICU1 is positioned within proximity of the C-terminal poly-aspartate tail of EMRE, allowing for putative salt-bridge formation.
source: This would position the N-terminal poly-basic region of MICU1 within the proximity of the C-terminal poly-aspartate tail of EMRE, allowing for the formation of a putative salt-bridge network (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The orientation of the α1 helix differs between the blocked and Ca2+-bound uniplex structures.
source: Although similar salt bridge interactions are also proposed in the Ca2+-bound uniplex structure, the orientation of the α1 helix is quite the opposite between the two structures.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the two structures.

claim: In the blocked uniplex, the C-terminus of the MICU1 α1 helix points toward the center of the channel.
source: In the blocked uniplex, the C-terminus of the MICU1 α1 helix points toward the center of the channel rather than away from the channel as seen in the Ca2+-bound structure.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: The α2 helix of MICU1 is positioned directly above the D-ring of MCU's selectivity filter in the blocked uniplex.
source: Secondly, the α2 helix is positioned directly above the D-ring of MCU's selectivity filter, which is formed by the four Asp261s from the DIME motif at the external entrance of the channel tetramer (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Several basic residues from MICU1 are in close proximity to the MCU D-ring and can potentially engage in electrostatic interactions.
source: Several basic residues from MICU1 are in close proximity and can potentially engage in electrostatic interactions with the MCU D-ring Asp261s, including K126 and R129 in α2 as well as the basic resides (R259, R261 and R263) in the loop between α7 and α8, which is disordered in the Ca2+-bound MICU1.
evidence: This is observed in the structure and inferred from the proximity of charged residues.

claim: Lys126 of MICU1 is well positioned to point its side chain directly toward the center of the D-ring and block the channel filter.
source: Most notably, Lys126 is well positioned to point its side chain directly toward the center of the D-ring and block the channel filter.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: The same electrostatic interactions between MICU1 and the MCU D-ring have been observed in a recent structure of the human uniplex obtained in low [Ca2+].
source: The same electrostatic interactions have been observed in the recent structure of the human uniplex obtained in low [Ca2+] (Fan et al., 2020) as well as the structure of a holocomplex formed by the beetle MCU-EMRE and the human MICU1-MICU2 under resting [Ca2+] conditions (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited recent structural studies.

claim: Mutations of positively charged residues in MICU1 that interact with the D-ring destabilize the MCU-MICU1 interactions and mitigate the blocking of MCU by MICU1.
source: In both studies, it has also been shown that mutations of these positively charged residues in MICU1 destabilize the MCU-MICU1 interactions and mitigate the blocking of MCU by MICU1.
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: The amphipathic C-terminal helix (C-helix, α17) of MICU1 lies on the membrane surface between two neighboring EMRE subunits in the blocked uniplex.
source: Thirdly, the amphipathic C-terminal helix (C-helix, α17) of MICU1 lies on the membrane surface between two neighboring EMRE subunits with its N-terminus sandwiched between the C-termini of an EMRE helix and the TM1 from a neighboring MCU subunit (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Van der Waals contacts mediate the interactions between MICU1's C-helix and MCU-EMRE.
source: Although the protein side chains are not resolved in the structure, the close proximity of multiple hydrophobic residues at this contact site would imply that van der Waals contacts mediate the interactions between MICU1's C-helix and MCU-EMRE.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement and the presence of hydrophobic residues.

claim: Deletion of MICU1's C-helix weakens the interaction between MCU and MICU1.
source: Deletion of MICU1's C-helix has been shown to weaken the interaction between MCU and MICU1 (Fan et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: A smaller class of apo uniplex particles reveals the unblocked uniporter with the MICU1-MICU2 heterotetramer bridging the two MCU-EMRE subcomplexes.
source: While the blocked uniporter represents the majority of the uniplex particles in the absence of Ca2+, a smaller class of particles reveals the unblocked uniporter with the MICU1-MICU2 heterotetramer bridging the two MCU-EMRE subcomplexes similar to that observed in the presence of high Ca2+ (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: In the apo, unblocked uniplex, the MCU-EMRE subcomplex part of the structure can be resolved to 3.7 Å.
source: In this apo, unblocked uniplex, the MCU-EMRE subcomplex part of the structure can be resolved to 3.7 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in the data processing workflow.

claim: The MICU1 and MICU2 parts of the apo, unblocked uniplex are poorly resolved, suggesting they are highly mobile and loosely attached to the MCU-EMRE subcomplex.
source: However, the MICU1 and MICU2 parts of the uniplex are poorly resolved in the EM map, suggesting that they are highly mobile and loosely attached to the MCU-EMRE subcomplex.
evidence: This is inferred from the poor resolution of the MICU1 and MICU2 density.

claim: The MICU1-MICU2 tetramer in the apo uniplex has an overall structural arrangement similar to that of the Ca2+-bound uniplex.
source: Intriguingly, the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer in the apo uniplex has an overall structural arrangement as that of the Ca2+-bound uniplex, but it does not appear to induce any movement to the MCU-EMRE subcomplexes whose V-shaped dimer structure remains identical to that determined without MICU1 and MICU2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The MICU1-MICU2 tetramer in the apo uniplex does not induce any movement to the MCU-EMRE subcomplexes.
source: Intriguingly, the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer in the apo uniplex has an overall structural arrangement as that of the Ca2+-bound uniplex, but it does not appear to induce any movement to the MCU-EMRE subcomplexes whose V-shaped dimer structure remains identical to that determined without MICU1 and MICU2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison.

claim: A similar apo, bridged uniplex structure is observed in a recent study of the human uniplex obtained in the absence of Ca2+.
source: Interestingly, similar apo, bridged uniplex structure is also observed in a recent study of the human uniplex obtained in the absence of Ca2+ (Zhuo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited recent structural study.

claim: The high degree of mobility exhibited by the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer in the apo, unblocked uniplex is evident in a class of particles where the bridging tetramer is pushed to the side due to competing binding of the blocking dimer.
source: The high degree of mobility exhibited by the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer in the apo, unblocked uniplex is also evident in another class of particles in which the bridging MICU1-MICU2 tetramer is pushed to the side of the MCU-EMRE subcomplex due to the competing binding of the MICU1-MICU2 dimer that occludes the channel pore (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The observation of the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer in a smaller subset of apo uniplex particles implies that the tetramer is not stable in the absence of Ca2+.
source: Nevertheless, the observation that the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer in a smaller subset of the apo uniplex particles and its weak association with the MCU-EMRE subcomplexes implies that the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer is not stable in the absence of Ca2+ and does not form tight contacts with the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the particle distribution and the poor resolution of MICU1-MICU2 in the apo bridged state.

claim: The structural changes within individual MICU1 or MICU2 subunit upon Ca2+ binding are quite subtle.
source: Comparison of uniplex structures with or without Ca2+ reveals that the Ca2+-induced conformational changes mainly occur within the MICU1-MICU2 dimer. The structural changes within individual MICU1 or MICU2 subunit are quite subtle with the most noticeable difference observed at the EF-1 motif where the two helices (α6 as the E1 helix and α7 as the F1 helix in both MICU1 and MICU2) are relatively parallel in the apo state but swing apart and become more perpendicular to each other in the Ca2+-bound state (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison shown in Figure 5a.

claim: At the EF-1 motif, the two helices are relatively parallel in the apo state but swing apart and become more perpendicular to each other in the Ca2+-bound state.
source: The structural changes within individual MICU1 or MICU2 subunit are quite subtle with the most noticeable difference observed at the EF-1 motif where the two helices (α6 as the E1 helix and α7 as the F1 helix in both MICU1 and MICU2) are relatively parallel in the apo state but swing apart and become more perpendicular to each other in the Ca2+-bound state (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structural comparison shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The conformational change at EF-1 results in a rearrangement of the hydrophobic contacts at the dimerization interface between MICU1 and MICU2.
source: As the EF-1 motifs from both MICU1 and MICU2 are directly involved in their face-to-face dimerization by forming hydrophobic interactions with the EF-3 motifs (α13 as the E3 helix and α14 as the F3 helix in both MICU1 and MICU2) from their respective partners, the conformational change at EF-1 results in a rearrangement of the hydrophobic contacts at the dimerization interface.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural changes at EF-1 and the known dimerization interface.

claim: MICU1 and MICU2 form a more compact dimer in the Ca2+-bound state.
source: Consequently, MICU1 and MICU2 form a more compact dimer in the Ca2+-bound state and their relative position also differs from that of the apo dimer (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is observed in the structural comparison shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The relative position of MICU1 and MICU2 differs between the apo and Ca2+-bound states.
source: Consequently, MICU1 and MICU2 form a more compact dimer in the Ca2+-bound state and their relative position also differs from that of the apo dimer (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is observed in the structural comparison shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The change in the relative position between MICU1 and MICU2 provides a structural explanation for the destabilization of channel blocking by MICU1-MICU2 upon Ca2+ binding.
source: The change in the relative position between MICU1 and MICU2 provides a plausible structural explanation for the destabilization of channel blocking by MICU1-MICU2 upon Ca2+ binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and functional context.

claim: If the Ca2+-bound MICU1-MICU2 dimer were to make the same blocking interactions as the apo dimer, the MICU2 subunit would clash with the C-helix of MICU1 or the membrane surface.
source: If we allow the Ca2+-bound MICU1-MICU2 dimer to make the same blocking interactions with MCU-EMRE as the apo dimer – by superimposing its MICU1 subunit onto the MICU1 of the apo blocked uniplex – then the MICU2 subunit would be positioned much closer to the membrane surface and its α11 helix would directly clash with the C-helix of MICU1 or the membrane surface (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural modeling shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The steric interference from the Ca2+-induced change at the MICU1-MICU2 interface would destabilize the blocking interaction and prevent the Ca2+-bound dimer from blocking the channel.
source: This steric interference implies that the Ca2+-induced change at the interfacial contact between MICU1 and MICU2, and the ensuing movement of MICU2 relative to MICU1, would destabilize the blocking interaction between MICU1 and MCU-EMRE and thus prevent the MICU1-MICU2 dimer from blocking the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural modeling and the observed steric clash.

claim: The MCU-EMRE subcomplex forms a dimer in the uniplex assembly, which likely represents a physiologically relevant state of the uniporter.
source: Here, we present multiple structures of the human uniplex consisting of MCU-EMRE-MICU1-MICU2 in the presence and absence of Ca2+. Consistent with our previous study (Wang et al., 2019), the MCU-EMRE subcomplex forms a dimer in the uniplex assembly, which likely represents a physiologically relevant state of the uniporter.
evidence: This is supported by the current structural data and a previous study.

claim: MICU1-MICU2 appears to be more stable as a heterodimer in the absence of Ca2+.
source: MICU1-MICU2 appears to be more stable as a heterodimer in the absence of Ca2+, but can further dimerize to form a heterotetramer upon Ca2+ binding through back-to-back dimerization between two MICU2 subunits.
evidence: This is observed in the particle distribution and structural data.

claim: MICU1-MICU2 can further dimerize to form a heterotetramer upon Ca2+ binding through back-to-back dimerization between two MICU2 subunits.
source: MICU1-MICU2 appears to be more stable as a heterodimer in the absence of Ca2+, but can further dimerize to form a heterotetramer upon Ca2+ binding through back-to-back dimerization between two MICU2 subunits.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structural data.

claim: No obvious structural change is observed at the MICU2-MICU2 homo-dimerization interface between the apo and Ca2+-bound states.
source: As no obvious structural change is observed at the MICU2-MICU2 homo-dimerization interface between the apo and Ca2+-bound states, it is unclear how Ca2+ binding promotes the tetramer formation.
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison.

claim: Ca2+ binding may promote tetramer formation by markedly stabilizing MICU2.
source: One possibility is that Ca2+ binding markedly stabilizes MICU2 as demonstrated in a thermal stability assay (Kamer et al., 2017), allowing it to have a more stable interface for dimerization.
evidence: This is speculated based on a cited thermal stability study.

claim: Initial studies showed that MCU exists in a large protein complex of ~500 kDa.
source: Major features of the uniplex structure help to reconcile some earlier experimental observations. First, initial studies showed that MCU exists in a large protein complex of ~500 kDa (Baughman et al., 2011; Sancak et al., 2013), which is compatible with the V-shaped MCU-EMRE subcomplex dimer bridged by a MICU1/MICU2 heterotetramer in the presence of Ca2+ or blocked by two MICU1-MICU2 dimers in the absence of Ca2+.
evidence: This is supported by cited initial studies and reconciled by the current structural data.

claim: The observed uniplex structures are compatible with the ~500 kDa complex size reported in initial studies.
source: Major features of the uniplex structure help to reconcile some earlier experimental observations. First, initial studies showed that MCU exists in a large protein complex of ~500 kDa (Baughman et al., 2011; Sancak et al., 2013), which is compatible with the V-shaped MCU-EMRE subcomplex dimer bridged by a MICU1/MICU2 heterotetramer in the presence of Ca2+ or blocked by two MICU1-MICU2 dimers in the absence of Ca2+.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the structural data with the reported complex size.

claim: Functional studies in knockout cell lines demonstrated non-equivalence of MICU1 and MICU2 at genetic and functional levels.
source: Second, functional studies in knockout cell lines using the HEK293T cell system have demonstrated non-equivalence of MICU1 and MICU2 both at a genetic level and at a functional level (Kamer and Mootha, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a cited functional study.

claim: The physical interaction between MCU and MICU2 requires the presence of MICU1.
source: Specifically, the physical interaction between MCU and MICU2 requires the presence of MICU1, however, MCU and MICU1 were able to interact in the absence of MICU2.
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies and explained by the structural data.

claim: MCU and MICU1 can interact in the absence of MICU2.
source: Specifically, the physical interaction between MCU and MICU2 requires the presence of MICU1, however, MCU and MICU1 were able to interact in the absence of MICU2.
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies and explained by the structural data.

claim: MICU1 is able to influence the threshold of calcium uptake by the uniporter independent of MICU2.
source: Genetic studies demonstrated that MICU1 is able to influence the threshold of calcium uptake by the uniporter independent of MICU2; however, the ability of MICU2 to do so required the presence of MICU1.
evidence: This is supported by cited genetic studies and explained by the structural data.

claim: The ability of MICU2 to influence the threshold of calcium uptake requires the presence of MICU1.
source: Genetic studies demonstrated that MICU1 is able to influence the threshold of calcium uptake by the uniporter independent of MICU2; however, the ability of MICU2 to do so required the presence of MICU1.
evidence: This is supported by cited genetic studies and explained by the structural data.

claim: The uniplex structure provides insight into the non-equivalence of MICU1 and MICU2.
source: The uniplex structure provides insight into this non-equivalence.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations showing different roles for MICU1 and MICU2.

claim: High-resolution structures of the MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer revealed that MICU2 is capable of engaging in both 'head-to-head' and 'back-to-back' interactions.
source: Third, recent high-resolution structures of the MICU1-MICU2 heterodimer have revealed that MICU2 is capable of engaging in 'head-to-head' interactions as well as 'back-to-back' interactions (Park et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited structural study.

claim: The observation of both head-to-head and back-to-back interactions of MICU2 is reconciled in the context of the MICU1-MICU2-MICU2-MICU1 bridge.
source: This was puzzling but is now reconciled in the context of the MICU1-MICU2-MICU2-MICU1 bridge between the V-shaped MCU-EMRE dimer.
evidence: This is explained by the current structural data showing the tetrameric arrangement.

claim: The MCU-EMRE subcomplex remains virtually identical in all uniplex structures.
source: The MCU-EMRE subcomplex, which functions as a conductive channel, remains virtually identical in all our uniplex structures, indicating that the binding of MICU1-MICU2 does not introduce any conformational change to the channel.
evidence: This is observed by comparing all the structures.

claim: The uniporter gating mechanism is defined by how MICU1-MICU2 interacts with MCU-EMRE in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: The uniporter gating mechanism is likely defined by how MICU1-MICU2 interacts with MCU-EMRE in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations of different interaction modes in different Ca2+ conditions.

claim: In the presence of Ca2+, the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer bridges the two MCU-EMRE subcomplexes without blocking the MCU channel pore.
source: In the presence of Ca2+, the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer bridges the two MCU-EMRE subcomplexes without blocking the MCU channel pore; electrostatic interactions between MICU1 and EMRE mediate this unblocked uniplex assembly.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structural data.

claim: Electrostatic interactions between MICU1 and EMRE mediate the unblocked uniplex assembly in the presence of Ca2+.
source: In the presence of Ca2+, the MICU1-MICU2 tetramer bridges the two MCU-EMRE subcomplexes without blocking the MCU channel pore; electrostatic interactions between MICU1 and EMRE mediate this unblocked uniplex assembly.
evidence: This is observed in the structure and inferred from the proximity of charged regions.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+, MICU1 from the MICU1-MICU2 dimer engages in more extensive interactions with both EMRE and the MCU pore, blocking the channel's external entrance.
source: In the absence of Ca2+, MICU1 from the MICU1-MICU2 dimer engages in more extensive interactions with both EMRE and the MCU pore of the MCU-EMRE subcomplex, blocking the channel's external entrance.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structural data.

claim: Because of the symmetry of the pore, the MICU1-MICU2 dimer can block the channel in four possible orientations.
source: Because of the symmetry of the pore, the MICU1-MICU2 dimer can block the channel in four possible orientations.
evidence: This is inferred from the four-fold symmetry of the MCU pore and observed in the data.

claim: A portion of the apo MICU1-MICU2 can dimerize to form a tetramer and bridge the MCU-EMRE subcomplex dimer without blocking the channel.
source: Interestingly, a portion of the apo MICU1-MICU2 can still dimerize to form a tetramer and bridge the MCU-EMRE subcomplex dimer without blocking the channel, similarly to the Ca2+-bound uniplex.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: The bridging assembly in the apo state does not appear to be as tight as that in the Ca2+-bound uniplex.
source: However, this bridging assembly in the apo state does not appear to be as tight as that in the Ca2+-bound uniplex.
evidence: This is inferred from the poor resolution and mobility of MICU1-MICU2 in the apo bridged state.

claim: The conversion between the apo, blocked and the bridged, unblocked uniplex assemblies involves the formation of completely different inter-protein contacts.
source: The conversion between the apo, blocked and the bridged, unblocked uniplex assemblies involves the formation of completely different inter-protein contacts and cannot be achieved by a simple conformational change.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison showing distinct interaction modes.

claim: To transition from blocked to unblocked state, MICU1-MICU2 has to first detach from the MCU-EMRE subcomplex and then re-attach at a different location.
source: In order to transition from one state to another, MICU1-MICU2 has to first detach from the MCU-EMRE subcomplex and then re-attach at a different location.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations showing completely different binding modes.

claim: The uniplex assembly with the apo MICU1-MICU2 dimer blocking the MCU pore prevails when cytosolic Ca2+ is low.
source: This leads to a simple working model for the gate-keeping mechanism of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter (Figure 6). The uniplex assembly with the apo MICU1-MICU2 dimer blocking the MCU pore prevails when cytosolic Ca2+ is low, mitigating Ca2+ uptake by the uniporter.
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the structural data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Upon elevation in cytosolic Ca2+, binding of Ca2+ to the EF-hands of MICU1-MICU2 triggers a conformational change at the MICU1-MICU2 dimerization interface.
source: Upon an elevation in cytosolic Ca2+, binding of Ca2+ to the EF-hands of MICU1-MICU2 triggers a conformational change at the MICU1-MICU2 dimerization interface and results in a downward movement of MICU2 that would directly interfere with MICU1's C-helix or the membrane surface.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: Ca2+ binding results in a downward movement of MICU2 that would interfere with MICU1's C-helix or the membrane surface.
source: Upon an elevation in cytosolic Ca2+, binding of Ca2+ to the EF-hands of MICU1-MICU2 triggers a conformational change at the MICU1-MICU2 dimerization interface and results in a downward movement of MICU2 that would directly interfere with MICU1's C-helix or the membrane surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural modeling showing steric clash.

claim: The steric interference from MICU2 movement prevents the dimer from maintaining its blocking interactions with the channel pore.
source: This steric interference prevents the dimer from maintaining its blocking interactions with the channel pore and causes the Ca2+-bound MICU1-MICU2 to dissociate from and disinhibit MCU.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The Ca2+-bound MICU1-MICU2 dissociates from and disinhibits MCU.
source: This steric interference prevents the dimer from maintaining its blocking interactions with the channel pore and causes the Ca2+-bound MICU1-MICU2 to dissociate from and disinhibit MCU.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The detached Ca2+-bound MICU1-MICU2 further dimerizes and re-attaches to the MCU-EMRE subcomplex to form a bridged uniplex with the unblocked channel pore.
source: The detached Ca2+-bound MICU1-MICU2 further dimerizes and re-attaches to the MCU-EMRE subcomplex to form a bridged uniplex with the unblocked channel pore.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The bridged uniplex assembly at high Ca2+ keeps MICU1-MICU2 in close proximity to the channel, making it readily available to block the MCU pore when Ca2+ levels return to resting concentration.
source: The bridged uniplex assembly at high Ca2+ keeps MICU1-MICU2 in close proximity to the channel, making it readily available to block the MCU pore when Ca2+ levels return to the resting concentration.
evidence: This is the proposed functional significance based on the structural observations.

claim: The results are consistent with the main findings from Fan et al., 2020, which showed a bridged, unblocked uniplex assembly at high Ca2+ and a blocked assembly under low Ca2+.
source: Among all those recently published uniplex structures (Fan et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Zhuo et al., 2020), our results are consistent with the main findings from that of Fan et al., 2020, which showed a bridged, unblocked uniplex assembly at high Ca2+ and a blocked assembly under low Ca2+.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with other published structures.

claim: A similar blocked uniplex structure was observed in the study by Wang et al., 2020, with an artificial assembly between beetle MCU-EMRE and human MICU1-MICU2.
source: A similar blocked uniplex structure was also observed in the study by Wang et al., 2020, even though the holocomplex is an artificial assembly between beetle MCU-EMRE and human MICU1-MICU2.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with other published structures.

claim: The structure by Zhuo et al., 2020 resembles the apo, bridged uniplex in this study.
source: The structure by Zhuo et al., 2020, which presumably represents the uniplex in the absence of Ca2+, appears to resemble that of the apo, bridged uniplex in our study.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with other published structures.

claim: The structural observation that MICU1 blocks MCU by directly blocking the ion conduction pathway in the absence of Ca2+ contradicts a recent electrophysiological analysis.
source: Our structural observation that MICU1 exerts its gating effect on MCU by directly blocking the ion conduction pathway in the absence of Ca2+ is in direct contradiction to the recent electrophysiological analysis of the uniporter (Garg et al., 2020), which argues that MICU1 does not block MCU at all.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with a conflicting functional study.

claim: More studies are needed to reconcile the discrepancies between structural and electrophysiological observations.
source: Given the current disagreement, more studies will be needed to reconcile these discrepancies.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion acknowledging the need for further research.
